clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in SCN2A encoding the voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit Nav1.2, expressed heavily in the axon initial segment of excitatory neurons during early development.

Age at seizure onset is the single most useful clinical clue to variant mechanism: early-infantile onset (typically first three months) usually reflects gain-of-function, whereas later onset (beyond around the first months) or non-epileptic autism/intellectual disability phenotypes usually reflect loss-of-function.

Early-onset gain-of-function cases characteristically respond to sodium-channel-blocking antiseizure medicines, while these same agents may worsen seizures in later-onset loss-of-function cases — making the phenotype-guided treatment split a defining feature.

Phenotypic spectrum spans benign familial infantile seizures, Ohtahara syndrome, epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures, and West syndrome, alongside autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability without epilepsy.
Episodic ataxia and later-onset movement phenomena are described, broadening the picture beyond seizures alone.
Most disease-causing variants arise de novo, though inherited variants underlie the milder self-limiting familial infantile seizure phenotype.
Neonatal or early-infantile tonic, focal, and migrating seizures with a burst-suppression or multifocal EEG should prompt sodium-channel gene testing including SCN2A.
Genotype-informed prescribing is central to management, so early genetic diagnosis materially changes the treatment pathway.
reference.pathophysiology: SCN2A encodes Nav1.2, a voltage-gated sodium channel alpha subunit concentrated in the axon initial segment and proximal axons of excitatory (glutamatergic) cortical and hippocampal neurons, where it drives action-potential initiation and propagation particularly in immature neurons before Nav1.6 predominates. Gain-of-function missense variants enhance channel activity — through increased persistent current, faster recovery from inactivation, or a hyperpolarising shift in activation — producing neuronal hyperexcitability that manifests as early-infantile seizures; because these channels are so critical in the neonatal period, such variants typically declare themselves in the first weeks to months of life and respond to sodium-channel blockade. Loss-of-function variants (including protein-truncating and some missense changes) reduce excitatory neuronal output; paradoxically this is associated with autism and intellectual disability, and when seizures occur they tend to begin later and may be aggravated by sodium-channel-blocking drugs, reflecting the developmental shift in channel expression. This mechanistic dichotomy — hyperfunction driving early seizures versus hypofunction driving neurodevelopmental impairment and later or drug-sensitive seizures — is the organising principle of the disorder and directly informs pharmacological choices.

redFlags: Neonatal-onset tonic or migrating focal seizures with burst-suppression EEG suggesting a severe early encephalopathy
Seizure worsening after introduction of a sodium-channel-blocking medicine, pointing to a loss-of-function mechanism
Developmental regression or arrest accompanying seizure onset
Recurrent status epilepticus or clustering of migrating focal seizures
Emerging feeding difficulty, apnoea, or autonomic instability in an encephalopathic infant
reference.prognosis: Outcome is highly variable and genotype-dependent, ranging from self-limiting familial infantile seizures with normal development to severe drug-resistant encephalopathy with profound intellectual disability. Early-onset gain-of-function seizures often improve with appropriate sodium-channel-blocking therapy, whereas loss-of-function phenotypes carry a substantial burden of autism and intellectual disability irrespective of seizure control.
pitfalls: Reflexively using or escalating a sodium-channel-blocking medicine in a later-onset case, which can aggravate loss-of-function seizures.
Assuming all SCN2A disease is epileptic and overlooking the autism/intellectual-disability-predominant loss-of-function phenotype without prominent seizures.
Attributing neonatal seizures to hypoxic-ischaemic injury and delaying genetic testing.
Failing to use age at onset as a guide to likely mechanism and therefore to drug selection.
Neglecting parental testing, leading to inaccurate recurrence-risk counselling for familial variants.
references: International consensus guidance on genetic epilepsies
management: Match antiseizure choice to the variant, using sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, or lacosamide for early-infantile gain-of-function seizures
Avoid sodium-channel blockers in later-onset loss-of-function phenotypes where they may aggravate seizures, selecting alternative agents
Trial vitamin-responsive epilepsy cofactors in neonatal presentations pending genetic confirmation
Escalate drug-resistant epilepsy with rational polytherapy and the ketogenic diet
Support autism and intellectual-disability phenotypes with developmental and behavioural intervention
Undertake parental testing and genetic counselling to establish de novo versus inherited status and recurrence risk
Refer to paediatric neurology and clinical genetics for phenotype-guided management
